skills.objective: Students read, write, compare and round decimals to the thousandths using place value, and add and subtract decimals by combining like places.
skills.studentObjective: I can use place value to read, compare, round, add and subtract decimals.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain which decimal is greater using because, but and so with the words place value, thousandths and greater than.
successCriteria: I name the place of every digit in a decimal, from tenths to thousandths.
I compare two decimals by writing them with the same number of places.
I round a decimal by looking at the digit one place to the right.
I add or subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points.
skills.bigIdea: Every place in a decimal is worth ten times the place to its right, so decimals are compared and combined one place at a time, not by how long they look.

syntax: ___ is greater than ___ because ___ tenths is more than ___ tenths.
The digit in the ___ place tells me to round up or stay.
discourse: Compare two decimals and defend which is greater
Explain the steps of rounding in the order they happen

domains.listening: Students listen to a plant-growth report and say which sprout is taller by hearing each place spoken aloud.
domains.speaking: Students read decimals aloud with place names, such as 4 and 382 thousandths, and tell a partner how they compared.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about timed flights and underline each decimal with the place it ends in.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares two decimals.

vocab.def: A number written with a point that separates whole units from parts smaller than one.
vocab.example: 4.75 has 4 ones and 75 hundredths
vocab.nonExample: 47, which has no point and no parts smaller than one
vocab.sentence: A decimal can name a part of a meter.
vocab.morphology: from Latin decem, meaning ten

vocab.def: The worth of a digit, which depends on where the digit sits in the number.
vocab.example: In 26.305, the 3 is in the tenths place and is worth 3 tenths
vocab.nonExample: Saying the 3 in 26.305 is worth 3 ones
vocab.sentence: Place value tells me the 5 in 0.05 is worth 5 hundredths.

vocab.def: Equal parts made by cutting one whole into 1,000 pieces; the third place after the point.
vocab.example: 0.007 is 7 thousandths
vocab.nonExample: 0.07, which is 7 hundredths
vocab.sentence: The thousandths place is the third digit after the point.
vocab.morphology: thousand + -ths, meaning one of a thousand equal parts

vocab.def: To replace a number with a nearby number that has fewer decimal places.
vocab.example: 7.46 rounds to 7.5 when we round to the nearest tenth
vocab.nonExample: Changing 7.46 to 7.4 by cutting off the 6
vocab.sentence: I round the decimal to the nearest tenth.
vocab.everyday: Shaped like a circle or a ball

vocab.def: A way to say one number is farther along the number line than another.
vocab.example: 0.6 is greater than 0.58
vocab.nonExample: 0.58 is greater than 0.6
vocab.sentence: Seven tenths is greater than six tenths.

misconceptions.belief: A decimal with more digits is a greater number.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the digits after the point like a whole number, so 58 looks bigger than 6.
misconceptions.fix: Write both decimals with the same number of places, then compare tenths first, using a number line or a grid to see the sizes.

errorCase.story: Tomás compares two ribbons that are 0.6 meter and 0.58 meter long.
steps: 0.6 has one digit after the point and 0.58 has two digits.
58 is greater than 6, so 0.58 is greater than 0.6.
So the 0.58 meter ribbon is longer.
errorCase.explain: Compare place by place. 0.6 is 6 tenths, which equals 60 hundredths. Since 60 hundredths is more than 58 hundredths, 0.6 is greater than 0.58.

misconceptions.belief: To add decimals, line up the last digits on the right.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number addition lines up the right edge, and students carry that habit to numbers with different amounts of places.
misconceptions.fix: Line up the decimal points first, then write a zero in any empty place so every column has the same kind of unit.

errorCase.story: Priya adds 2.4 and 0.35.
steps: I line up the last digits, so the 4 sits above the 5.
Then I add the columns: 4 + 5 = 9 and 2 + 3 = 5, so the sum is 5.9.
errorCase.explain: The 4 is in the tenths place and the 5 is in the hundredths place, so they cannot be added together. Line up the points: 2.40 + 0.35 = 2.75.

misconceptions.belief: To round to the tenths, look at the last digit of the number.
misconceptions.why: Students learn 'look at the next digit' as 'look at the end', which works only when the number has no extra places.
misconceptions.fix: Circle the place you are rounding to, then draw an arrow to the single digit just to its right and decide using only that digit.

errorCase.story: Dani rounds 3.462 to the nearest tenth.
steps: I want to round 3.462 to the nearest tenth.
I look at the last digit, 2, which is less than 5.
So the tenths digit stays and the answer is 3.4.
errorCase.explain: Rounding to tenths depends on the hundredths digit, which is 6. Since 6 is 5 or more, 3.462 rounds up to 3.5.

misconceptions.belief: Hundredths are greater than tenths because 100 is greater than 10.
misconceptions.why: The words hundredths and tenths sound like the whole numbers, and the ending -ths is easy to miss, so the size of the piece is reversed.
misconceptions.fix: Fold a strip into 10 equal parts and then 100 equal parts, and say aloud that more parts means each part is smaller.

reading.title: Paper Airplanes in the Gym
reading.text: Rosa and Kenji time their paper airplanes in the school gym. Rosa's plane stays in the air for 4.382 seconds. Kenji's plane stays up for 4.38 seconds. Kenji says his decimal is greater, because hundredths are bigger pieces than thousandths. Rosa uses place value to check. She writes both decimals with three places: 4.382 and 4.380. The ones, tenths and hundredths digits match, so she compares the thousandths. Since 2 thousandths is greater than 0 thousandths, her plane flew longer. The class chart has room for only one decimal place, so the friends round each time to the nearest tenth. The hundredths digit in both times is 8, which is 5 or more, so both times round to 4.4 seconds.
reading.simple: Rosa and Kenji time paper airplanes. Rosa's plane flies 4.382 seconds. Kenji's plane flies 4.38 seconds. Kenji says his decimal is greater. Rosa uses place value. She writes 4.38 as 4.380 so both have the same places. The thousandths are 2 and 0. 2 thousandths is greater than 0 thousandths, so her plane flew longer. The chart shows tenths only, so they round. The hundredths digit is 8, which is 5 or more. Both times round to 4.4 seconds.

questions.q: How long did Kenji's plane stay in the air?
questions.a: 4.38 seconds

questions.q: Why does Rosa write 4.38 as 4.380 before she compares?
questions.a: Then both decimals have thousandths, so she can compare the same places.

questions.q: Both times round to the nearest tenth. What is the rounded time, and which digit decided it?
questions.a: 4.4 seconds. The hundredths digit, 8, is 5 or more, so the tenths digit goes up.

wdntb.why: 0.05 is 5 hundredths, but the other three all name 5 tenths with different numbers of zeros.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at these lengths of string: 2.5 cm, 2.50 cm, 2.05 cm and 2.055 cm. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Writing a zero at the end of a decimal after the point changes its value.
asn.why: 0.7 and 0.70 both name 7 tenths. A zero at the end only adds an empty smaller place.

asn.claim: A decimal with more digits after the point is greater than a decimal with fewer digits.
asn.why: 0.45 is greater than 0.4, but 0.45 is less than 0.5. The places decide, not the number of digits.

wyr.q: Would you rather compare 0.8 and 0.75 on a number line or by writing both with two places?

compare.a: Lena writes 0.8 as 0.80 and compares 80 hundredths with 75 hundredths.
compare.b: Matt says 0.75 is greater because 75 is greater than 8.
compare.prompt: Which strategy tells you which decimal is greater? How do you know?

debate.claim: Rounding changes the number, so it is never a good idea to round.
debate.forEvidence: Rounding 4.382 to 4.4 loses the thousandths, so the new number is not the same as the real time.
debate.againstEvidence: A chart with one decimal place is easier to read, and 4.4 is very close to the real time.

listening.script: Welcome, plant scientists. Amara measures two bean sprouts for her class. Sprout A is 3.5 centimeters tall. Sprout B is 3.45 centimeters tall. Amara says, Sprout B is taller, because 45 is more than 5. Let us listen to the places. Three point five is three and five tenths. Three point four five is three and four tenths and five hundredths. Write 3.5 as 3.50. Fifty hundredths is more than forty-five hundredths. So Sprout A is taller by five hundredths of a centimeter.

tasks.q: Which sprout is taller?
tasks.why: 3.5 is 3.50, and 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths.

tasks.q: What mistake did Amara make?
options: She compared 45 and 5 as whole numbers without matching the places.
She forgot to round to the nearest tenth.
She read the decimal point as a comma.
tasks.why: The 5 in 3.5 is in the tenths place, but the 5 in 3.45 is in the hundredths place.

story.title: The Seed Scale
story.goal: record the mass of each seed packet correctly on the garden chart
story.intro: Kofi weighs seed packets for the spring garden. The scale shows grams with three decimal places, and the chart needs every mass written carefully so the gardeners plant the right amounts.

beats.lead: Kofi reads the first packet from the display and starts to write it on the chart.
beats.success: Kofi writes each digit in its place, and the first packet is recorded correctly.
beats.redirect: A digit landed in the wrong place on the chart, so Kofi says the place names aloud and writes it again.

beats.lead: Two packets look almost the same on the scale, and Kofi has to decide which one is heavier.
beats.success: Kofi writes both masses with the same places and finds the heavier packet.
beats.redirect: The packets are still mixed up, so Kofi lines up the places and compares tenths first.

beats.lead: The garden club wants the chart rounded so it fits on one small poster.
beats.success: Kofi circles the place, checks the digit to its right and rounds every mass the right way.
beats.redirect: The poster numbers look off, so Kofi checks the digit just to the right of the place being rounded.

story.ending: The garden chart is clear and correct, and Kofi can explain how each decimal was read, compared and rounded.

panels.says: My long jump was 1.39 meters and Ivy's was 1.4 meters. Mine is longer, because 139 is more than 14.
Let us line up the places. I can write 1.4 as 1.40.
Now I see 1.39 and 1.40. Forty hundredths is more than 39 hundredths.
So my jump is longer by one hundredth of a meter.

predict.q: Before Ivy answers, predict whose jump is longer.
predict.why: 1.4 is the same as 1.40, and 40 hundredths is more than 39 hundredths.

transfer.relationship: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right
phrasings: A digit is worth 10 times the same digit one place to its right
The 5 in 0.5 is worth 10 times the 5 in 0.05
Moving one place right divides a digit's value by 10
5 tenths is the same amount as 50 hundredths

decoys.text: A digit is worth 10 times the same digit one place to its left
decoys.why: This reverses the direction, so it says the greater place is on the right.

decoys.text: The 5 in 0.05 is worth more than the 5 in 0.5 because it is written farther right
decoys.why: Moving right makes the place smaller, not greater.

modeling.title: Reading a rain gauge
modeling.scenario: A fictional class keeps a rain gauge on the school roof. On three days in one week they record how many centimeters of rain fell.
assumptions: The gauge was emptied before each day began.
Each reading is exact to the hundredths place.
Only these three days are in the total.
prompts: What is the total rain for the three days? Line up the decimal points before you add.
How much more rain fell on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
Round each day to the nearest tenth and add. Does the rounded total match the exact total?
limits: A real rain gauge can be read only as exactly as its marks allow.
Wind can blow rain away, so these amounts may be a little low.

sentence.because: The decimal 0.6 is greater than 0.58 because 6 tenths equals 60 hundredths, and 60 hundredths is more than 58 hundredths.
sentence.but: The decimal 0.58 has more digits, but 0.6 is greater than 0.58.
sentence.so: Six tenths equals 60 hundredths, so 0.6 is greater than 0.58.

diagnostic.prompt: Place 0.7 and 0.65 on a number line from 0 to 1. Tell which is greater and how you know.
lookFor: Puts 0.7 to the right of 0.65 on the line
Writes 0.7 as 0.70 or 70 hundredths to compare
Names the place that decides, tenths or hundredths
diagnostic.language: Let the student point to the number line and write the zeros before speaking. If the line is correct but the explanation is short, the barrier is language, not place value.

extension.task: Find a decimal that is greater than 0.43 and less than 0.44. Then find two more.
extension.reasoning: Explain why there is always another decimal between any two decimals, using thousandths in your argument.

en.learning: Your child is learning to read, compare and round decimals with tenths, hundredths and thousandths, like a time of 4.382 seconds.
en.say: To compare two decimals, write both with the same number of places and compare one place at a time, starting on the left.
en.ask: Which is greater, 0.6 or 0.58? How do you know?
en.activity: Look at prices on a store receipt or flyer together. Pick two prices with cents and ask your child which is more and by how much.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a leer, comparar y redondear decimales con décimas, centésimas y milésimas, como un tiempo de 4.382 segundos.
es.say: Para comparar dos decimales, escriban los dos con la misma cantidad de cifras y comparen lugar por lugar, empezando por la izquierda.
es.activity: Miren juntos los precios de un recibo o de un anuncio de la tienda. Escojan dos precios con centavos y pregunten cuál cuesta más y cuánto más.

skills.objective: Students add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by renaming them as equivalent fractions, multiply fractions and whole numbers, and divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
skills.studentObjective: I can add, subtract, multiply and share fractions, and I can explain each answer with a picture or an equation.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I combined or shared fractions using because, but and so with the words common denominator, equivalent fractions and product.
successCriteria: I rename fractions with a common denominator before I add or subtract them.
I multiply a fraction by a whole number or by another fraction and show it with an area model.
I share a unit fraction equally and write the answer as a division equation.
I explain in a full sentence why my answer is reasonable.
skills.bigIdea: Fractions are added when their pieces are the same size, and they are multiplied or divided when we take a part of a part or share a part equally.

syntax: I renamed ___ as ___ so the pieces are the same size.
The product of ___ and ___ is ___ because I took ___ of ___.
discourse: Explain each step of adding fractions in the order it happens
Justify why an answer is greater or less than the number you started with

domains.listening: Students listen to a plan for sharing a granola bar and say what fraction each person gets.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they renamed the fractions and why the pieces must match before adding.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about painting a fence and mark each fraction with what it measures.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that justifies a sum or a product.

vocab.def: The bottom number in a fraction; it tells how many equal parts make one whole.
vocab.example: In 3/8, the denominator is 8
vocab.nonExample: In 3/8, the 3 is not the denominator
vocab.sentence: The denominator tells the size of each piece.
vocab.morphology: from Latin nomen, meaning name; the denominator names the kind of piece

vocab.def: A denominator that two or more fractions share, so their pieces are the same size.
vocab.example: 6 is a common denominator for 1/2 and 1/3
vocab.nonExample: 2 and 3, the separate denominators of 1/2 and 1/3
vocab.sentence: I find a common denominator before I add.

vocab.def: Fractions with different names that show the same amount.
vocab.sentence: I rename 1/2 as 3/6 by using equivalent fractions.
vocab.morphology: equi- means equal; valent means worth

vocab.def: The answer you get when you multiply two numbers or fractions.
vocab.example: The product of 1/2 and 1/6 is 1/12
vocab.nonExample: The sum of 1/2 and 1/6, which comes from adding
vocab.sentence: The product of 1/2 and 1/6 is 1/12.
vocab.everyday: Something that is made or grown to be sold, like cereal or oranges
vocab.morphology: from Latin producere, meaning to bring forth

visual.caption: A product is the result of multiplying

vocab.def: A fraction with 1 on top that shows one equal part of a whole.
vocab.example: 1/6 is one of six equal parts
vocab.nonExample: 5/6, which is five of six equal parts
vocab.sentence: A unit fraction names a single piece.

misconceptions.belief: To add fractions, add the numerators and add the denominators.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number addition works one column at a time, and students apply the same pattern to the top and bottom numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Fold two strips, one into halves and one into thirds, and show that the pieces must be renamed to the same size before they can be counted together.

errorCase.story: Jada eats 1/2 of a pizza and then 1/3 of a second pizza of the same size.
steps: Halves and thirds are two different sizes of piece.
I add the numerators and the denominators: 1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 3 = 5.
errorCase.explain: Pieces can be added only when they are the same size. Rename as sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the sum is 5/6. A quick check: 2/5 is less than 1/2, so it cannot be the sum of two parts.

misconceptions.belief: To multiply a whole number by a fraction, multiply the top and the bottom by the whole number.
misconceptions.why: Students remember to multiply across and forget that the whole number is a count of groups, not a new size of piece.
misconceptions.fix: Draw 4 groups of one fifth on a strip, then count the fifths aloud: four fifths. Compare the size of the piece before and after.

errorCase.story: Kai wants 4 groups of 1/5 of a cup of seeds.
steps: I need 4 groups of 1/5.
I multiply both numbers by 4: 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 × 5 = 20.
errorCase.explain: 4 groups of 1 fifth is 4 fifths, so the product is 4/5. The size of the piece stays fifths and only the count changes. 4/20 equals 1/5, and 4 groups cannot be the same as 1 group.

misconceptions.belief: To share a unit fraction among some people, divide the number of people by the fraction.
misconceptions.why: Division facts in whole numbers put the larger number first, so students reverse the order of the problem.
misconceptions.fix: Cut a strip showing 1/3 into 4 equal shares and name the size of one share as part of the whole strip.

errorCase.story: Mia has 1/3 of a pan of rice and shares it equally among 4 friends.
steps: I divide the 1/3 pan into 4 equal shares.
So each friend gets 12 pans.
errorCase.explain: The problem is 1/3 ÷ 4, not 4 ÷ 1/3. Cutting 1/3 into 4 parts makes 12 equal pieces in the whole pan, so each friend gets 1/12 of the pan. A share cannot be more than the whole pan.

misconceptions.belief: In '2/3 of 12', the word of tells me to add.
misconceptions.why: Students know of from phrases like 'a cup of milk', where it names a container, so they do not read it as 'a part of this amount'.
misconceptions.fix: Draw 12 counters, circle 3 equal groups, shade 2 groups, and say aloud: two thirds of twelve is eight.

reading.title: Painting the Garden Fence
reading.text: Eli and his sister Noor are painting a long garden fence. On Saturday, Eli paints 1/2 of the fence. On Sunday, Noor paints 1/3 of the fence. To find how much is painted, they need a common denominator, because halves and thirds are different sizes. They rename both amounts as equivalent fractions: 1/2 is 3/6 and 1/3 is 2/6. Together they painted 5/6 of the fence. That leaves 1/6, which is a unit fraction. On Monday, the two share that last piece equally, so each paints 1/6 ÷ 2, which is 1/12 of the fence. Noor notices that half of 1/6 gives the same answer as the product of 1/2 and 1/6.
reading.simple: Eli and Noor are painting a fence. Eli paints 1/2 of the fence. Noor paints 1/3 of the fence. Halves and thirds are different sizes, so they find a common denominator. They write equivalent fractions: 1/2 is 3/6 and 1/3 is 2/6. Together they painted 5/6 of the fence. The unit fraction 1/6 is left. They share it equally. Each paints 1/6 ÷ 2, which is 1/12 of the fence. The product of 1/2 and 1/6 is the same.

questions.q: How much of the fence is left after Saturday and Sunday?
questions.a: 1/6 of the fence

questions.q: Why do Eli and Noor rename the fractions as sixths before they add?
questions.a: Halves and thirds are different-sized pieces. Sixths are the same size for both, so the pieces can be counted together.

questions.q: How much of the whole fence does each person paint on Monday?
questions.a: 1/12 of the fence, because 1/6 shared equally by 2 people is 1/6 ÷ 2 = 1/12.

wdntb.why: 2/5 is the only one that is not 5/6. The first three name the same amount, so 2/5 is the odd one out.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at these equations: 1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, and 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The product of two fractions that are each less than 1 is less than both of them.
asn.why: Taking a part of a part gives a smaller amount, like 1/2 of 1/6 being 1/12.

asn.claim: When you add two fractions with different denominators, the sum has the same denominator as one of them.
asn.why: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, which has a denominator of 4. But 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, and 6 is neither 2 nor 3.

wyr.q: Would you rather find 1/2 of 1/6 with an area model or by multiplying numerators and denominators?

compare.a: Sam finds 1/2 + 1/3 by renaming both as sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
compare.b: Tia finds 1/2 + 1/3 by renaming both as twelfths: 6/12 + 4/12 = 10/12, which is 5/6.
compare.prompt: Both strategies give the same sum. Why can different common denominators both work?

debate.claim: You must always use the least common denominator to add fractions.
debate.forEvidence: The least common denominator keeps the numbers small, as in 5/6 instead of 10/12.
debate.againstEvidence: Any common denominator works. Twelfths give 6/12 + 4/12 = 10/12, which is equal to 5/6.

listening.script: Listen to Imani's plan for her granola bar. I have three fourths of a bar. I want to give half of my piece to my brother. So I need half of three fourths. First I cut every fourth into two equal pieces, and now the whole bar has eight equal pieces. My piece is six of those eighths. Half of six pieces is three pieces. My brother gets three eighths of the whole bar. That is less than three fourths, because he gets only part of my piece.

tasks.q: What fraction of the whole bar does Imani's brother get?
tasks.why: Half of 6 eighths is 3 eighths of the whole bar.

tasks.q: What happens when Imani cuts every fourth into two equal pieces?
options: The whole bar has 8 equal pieces.
The whole bar has 6 equal pieces.
The whole bar has 2 equal pieces.
tasks.why: 4 fourths cut in two each make 4 × 2 = 8 equal pieces.

story.title: Soup for the Supper
story.goal: prepare enough vegetable soup for the Friday supper
story.intro: Mateo helps cook at the community kitchen. The recipe cards use fractions of a pot, so Mateo has to combine and share the amounts carefully before the families arrive.

beats.lead: Mateo has two bowls of broth in different measures and needs to know how much he has in all.
beats.success: Mateo renames both amounts with the same denominator and finds the right total.
beats.redirect: The total looks too small, so Mateo checks that the pieces he added are the same size.

beats.lead: A neighbor asks for a part of one portion, and Mateo has to take a fraction of a fraction.
beats.success: Mateo draws the area model and finds the part of the part without losing the whole.
beats.redirect: The share is too big, so Mateo draws the model again and checks the answer against both factors.

beats.lead: One last pot has to be shared equally among a few volunteers.
beats.success: Mateo cuts the amount into equal shares and writes the division that matches.
beats.redirect: The shares do not fit, so Mateo checks which amount is being divided and which is the number of people.

story.ending: The supper is ready on time, and Mateo can explain how every fraction was added, taken and shared.

panels.says: I read 1/4 of my book on Monday and 2/3 of it on Tuesday.
I will add straight across: 1 + 2 = 3 and 4 + 3 = 7, so you read 3/7.
Wait. Fourths and thirds are different sizes. Let us rename both as twelfths.
Now I see it. 1/4 is 3/12 and 2/3 is 8/12, so that makes 11/12.

predict.q: Before Lina answers, predict how much of the book she read in all.
predict.why: Renamed as twelfths, 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12. The answer 3/7 is less than 2/3 alone, so it cannot be the sum.

transfer.relationship: Taking half of one sixth makes a piece that is one twelfth of the whole
phrasings: Half of one sixth of the fence
One sixth shared equally by 2 people

decoys.why: This doubles the amount, so it finds 2 sixths instead of half of a sixth.
This adds a sixth and a half, which makes a bigger amount instead of a smaller one.

modeling.title: Fruit punch for family night
modeling.scenario: A fictional class makes fruit punch for a family night. They have two juices, and they need to measure, combine and share them.
assumptions: No juice is spilled while pouring.
Every cup is filled to exactly 1/4 liter.
The orange juice, the pineapple juice and the water are kept in separate containers.
prompts: How many liters of juice does the class have when the two juices are combined?
The class pours the 1/2 liter of orange juice equally into 3 bottles. How much is in each bottle?
How many cups of 1/4 liter can the class fill with 2 liters of water?
limits: Real cups are never filled to exactly the same level, so some cups may hold a little more or less.
We did not decide how sweet the punch should taste, which would change how much water to add.

sentence.because: The sum of 1/2 and 1/3 is 5/6 because both fractions can be renamed as sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
sentence.but: The denominators 2 and 3 are different, but 1/2 and 1/3 can still be added after renaming.
sentence.so: Both fractions are renamed as sixths, so the sum of 1/2 and 1/3 is 5/6.

diagnostic.prompt: Find 1/2 + 1/3 and also 1/2 × 1/3. Draw a picture for each one and tell how the two answers are different.
lookFor: Renames halves and thirds as sixths before adding
Gets 5/6 for the sum and 1/6 for the product
Explains that the product is a part of a part, so it is smaller than either fraction
diagnostic.language: Let the student draw and label the pieces first. If both pictures are correct and the student cannot yet say why, the barrier is language, not fractions.

extension.task: Write a story problem for 2/3 × 3/4. Solve it with an area model, then check that the answer is less than each factor.
extension.reasoning: Explain, using a drawing, why 4 ÷ 1/5 is 20 but 1/5 ÷ 4 is 1/20.

en.learning: Your child is learning to add, subtract, multiply and share fractions, like finding half of 1/4 of a cake.
en.say: To add halves and thirds, cut both into pieces of the same size, such as sixths.
en.ask: If we eat 1/2 of a cake today and 1/3 of the same cake tomorrow, how much of the cake did we eat?
en.activity: Fold a paper strip in half, then fold the doubled strip into three equal parts. Unfold it, count the equal pieces and ask what fraction of the strip each piece is.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a sumar, restar, multiplicar y repartir fracciones, como hallar la mitad de 1/4 de un pastel.
es.say: Para sumar mitades y tercios, corten las dos fracciones en piezas del mismo tamaño, como sextos.
es.ask: Si hoy comemos 1/2 de un pastel y mañana 1/3 del mismo pastel, ¿qué parte del pastel comimos?
es.activity: Doblen una tira de papel por la mitad y luego doblen esa mitad en tres partes iguales. Desdoblen la tira, cuenten las piezas iguales y pregunten qué fracción de la tira es cada pieza.

skills.objective: Students evaluate numerical expressions that use parentheses with the agreed order of operations, and write and interpret expressions from words without evaluating them.
skills.studentObjective: I can write an expression from words and find its value by doing the steps in the right order.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why the parentheses change an expression using because, but and so with the words expression, parentheses and order of operations.
successCriteria: I evaluate what is inside parentheses before I do anything else.
I multiply and divide before I add and subtract when there are no parentheses.
I write an expression that matches a sentence, such as 'add 6 and 3, then multiply by 4'.
I say how an expression changes in meaning when parentheses are added or removed.
skills.bigIdea: An expression is a short way to write a plan with numbers, and the parentheses and the order of operations tell everyone which step to do first.

syntax: First I ___, then I ___, and last I ___.
The expression ___ means ___ because the parentheses group ___.
discourse: Describe the steps of a calculation in the order they happen
Compare two expressions with the same numbers but different values

domains.listening: Students listen to a classmate read two expressions aloud and write each one with the parentheses in the right place.
domains.speaking: Students say an expression in words, using phrases like the sum of and times, and a partner writes it.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about book fair costs and circle the expressions and the steps for each.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that explains why two expressions differ.

vocab.def: A group of numbers and operation signs that shows a quantity, with no equal sign.
vocab.nonExample: 3 × 4 = 12, which has an equal sign and an answer
vocab.sentence: I write an expression to show the cost.
vocab.morphology: from Latin exprimere, meaning to press out or show

vocab.def: Curved marks that group part of an expression so that part is done first.
vocab.nonExample: 5 × 4 + 1, which has no grouping marks
vocab.sentence: The parentheses show which step comes first.

vocab.def: A mathematical action, such as adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing.
vocab.example: Multiplication is an operation
vocab.nonExample: The number 12, which is a value and not an action
vocab.sentence: Each operation in the expression gets its own step.
vocab.everyday: A medical procedure done by a surgeon in a hospital

vocab.def: To find the value of an expression by doing the operations in the correct order.
vocab.example: Evaluate 3 + 4 × 2 to get 11
vocab.nonExample: Writing 3 + 4 × 2 without finding a value
vocab.sentence: I evaluate the expression one step at a time.
vocab.morphology: from Latin valere, meaning to be worth

vocab.def: The agreed order for doing steps: parentheses first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
vocab.example: In 3 + 4 × 2, multiply first to get 3 + 8
vocab.nonExample: Working strictly from left to right to get 14
vocab.sentence: The order of operations tells me that multiplication comes before addition.

misconceptions.belief: Always work from left to right, whatever the operations are.
misconceptions.why: Students read left to right in every other subject, and early addition-only practice never showed a reason to do anything else.
misconceptions.fix: Show the cost of 3 pens plus 1 pack of 2 pens at 4 dollars each as a story, and let the story, not the reading direction, decide which step is done first.

errorCase.story: Noa evaluates the expression 3 + 4 × 2.
steps: The expression is 3 + 4 × 2, and it has no parentheses.
I work from left to right: 3 + 4 = 7.
errorCase.explain: With no parentheses, multiplication comes before addition. First 4 × 2 = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11.

misconceptions.belief: Parentheses are only decoration, so the value is the same with or without them.
misconceptions.why: The curved marks look small, and students do not yet see that they group a quantity that must be found as one piece.
misconceptions.fix: Build 3 groups of (6 + 4) with counters and show that the grouping makes 3 groups of 10, not 3 groups of 6 plus 4 extra.

errorCase.story: Eli evaluates 3 × (6 + 4).
steps: The expression is 3 × (6 + 4).
I multiply first: 3 × 6 = 18.
Then I add 4: 18 + 4 = 22.
errorCase.explain: The parentheses say to find 6 + 4 = 10 first. Then 3 × 10 = 30.

misconceptions.belief: To write 'subtract 5 from 12', write the numbers in the order you hear them.
misconceptions.why: In English, subtract 5 from 12 puts 5 before 12 in the sentence, but the expression starts with the 12.
misconceptions.fix: Act it out with 12 counters and take away 5, and say aloud 'start with 12, take away 5'.

errorCase.story: Rosa writes an expression for 'subtract 5 from 12'.
steps: I see the numbers 5 and 12 and the word subtract.
I write the numbers in the order I hear them: 5 − 12.
So the expression is 5 − 12.
errorCase.explain: Subtract 5 from 12 means start with 12 and take away 5, so the expression is 12 − 5 and its value is 7. The word from tells which number to start with.

misconceptions.belief: 'Twice the sum of 3 and 4' is written 2 × 3 + 4.
misconceptions.why: Students attach twice to the nearest number and do not read the sum of 3 and 4 as one quantity that gets doubled.
misconceptions.fix: Say the phrase in pieces, 'the sum of 3 and 4' first, and write that piece inside parentheses before adding the word twice.

reading.title: Costs at the Book Fair
reading.text: At the book fair, Dara buys 3 books that cost 4 dollars each and 2 bookmarks that cost 1 dollar each. She writes the expression 3 × 4 + 2 × 1. To evaluate it, she follows the order of operations. Multiplication comes before addition, so 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 1 = 2, and the total is 12 + 2 = 14 dollars. Her friend Lucas buys one book and one bookmark for each of 5 friends. He writes 5 × (4 + 1). The parentheses show that the cost of one gift is found first: 4 + 1 = 5. Then 5 × 5 = 25 dollars. Without the parentheses, 5 × 4 + 1 would be 21, which is a different amount.
reading.simple: Dara buys 3 books that cost 4 dollars each and 2 bookmarks that cost 1 dollar each. Her expression is 3 × 4 + 2 × 1. Multiplication comes first. 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 1 = 2. Then 12 + 2 = 14 dollars. Lucas buys one book and one bookmark for each of 5 friends. His expression is 5 × (4 + 1). Parentheses mean add first: 4 + 1 = 5. Then 5 × 5 = 25 dollars. Without parentheses, 5 × 4 + 1 would be 21.

questions.q: How much does Dara spend in all?
questions.a: 14 dollars

questions.q: Why does Lucas put parentheses around 4 + 1?
questions.a: One gift costs 4 + 1 dollars, and he needs 5 of those gifts, so the cost of one gift must be found first.

questions.q: Why is 5 × 4 + 1 equal to 21, and not 25?
questions.a: Multiplication comes first: 5 × 4 = 20, then 20 + 1 = 21. Only the books are multiplied by 5.

wdntb.why: (2 + 3) × 4 equals 20, but the other three all have the value 14.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at these two expressions: 6 + 3 × 4 and (6 + 3) × 4. They use the same numbers and signs. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Putting parentheses around the first two numbers in an expression never changes its value.
asn.why: In 2 + 3 + 4 the value stays 9. But in 2 + 3 × 4 it changes the value from 14 to 20.

asn.claim: Multiplication is done before addition, unless parentheses say to do something else first.
asn.why: This is the agreed order of operations, so everyone who evaluates 3 + 4 × 2 gets the same value, 11.

wyr.q: Would you rather write 'add 6 and 3, then multiply by 4' as an expression or draw it as a picture of 4 groups?

compare.a: Ines evaluates 8 + 6 ÷ 2 by doing 6 ÷ 2 = 3 first, and then 8 + 3 = 11.
compare.b: Bo evaluates 8 + 6 ÷ 2 from left to right: 8 + 6 = 14, and then 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
compare.prompt: Which strategy follows the order of operations? How do you know?

debate.claim: We should always use parentheses, so nobody has to remember the order of operations.
debate.forEvidence: Parentheses make the plan clear, as in 8 + (6 ÷ 2), so nobody has to guess which step is first.
debate.againstEvidence: Too many parentheses make an expression long and hard to read, and the order of operations already gives one clear answer.

listening.script: Listen to Tariq read two expressions. The first is two times the sum of eight and seven. I write the sum in parentheses, two times parentheses eight plus seven. The sum is fifteen, and two times fifteen is thirty. The second is the sum of two times eight, and seven. I write that as two times eight, plus seven. Two times eight is sixteen, and sixteen plus seven is twenty-three. The numbers and the signs are the same, but the answers are different, because the parentheses group different parts.

tasks.q: What is the value of 2 × (8 + 7)?
tasks.why: The sum 8 + 7 = 15 is found first, and 2 × 15 = 30.

tasks.q: Which expression matches the words 'the sum of two times eight, and seven'?
tasks.why: Two times eight is found first, and then seven is added, so no parentheses are needed.

story.title: The Science Fair Budget
story.goal: show the cost of the club's supplies on a poster with clear expressions
story.intro: Ayla's team is building a poster for the science fair. The judges want to see the cost of the supplies written as expressions, and every expression must give the same total as the receipts.

beats.lead: Ayla reads the receipt aloud and starts to write the cost of the first supplies as an expression.
beats.success: Ayla writes an expression that matches the words on the receipt, so the judges can follow it.
beats.redirect: The expression does not match the receipt, so Ayla says the plan in words and writes it again.

beats.lead: Her partner writes a second expression with the same numbers and gets a different total.
beats.success: Ayla and her partner find where the parentheses go, and both totals now agree.
beats.redirect: The totals still differ, so they check which step the parentheses say to do first.

beats.lead: The judges ask Ayla to explain how she found one of the totals.
beats.success: Ayla explains each step in order and names the order of operations she used.
beats.redirect: The explanation skips a step, so Ayla goes back through the expression one operation at a time.

story.ending: The poster is clear and correct, and Ayla can explain why each expression has the value it has.

panels.says: I think 10 − 2 × 3 is 24, because 10 − 2 = 8 and 8 × 3 = 24.
Multiplication comes first. 2 × 3 = 6, and then 10 − 6 = 4.
Then how would I write the 24 I found?
You need parentheses: (10 − 2) × 3. They change the order.

predict.q: Before Rin answers, predict the value of 10 − 2 × 3 when there are no parentheses.

transfer.relationship: Find the amount in the group first, then multiply it by the number of groups
phrasings: 5 groups of (4 plus 1)
Multiply 5 by the sum of 4 and 1
5 gifts, each with a 4-dollar book and a 1-dollar bookmark

decoys.why: Only the books are multiplied by 5, and the one bookmark is counted once.
This adds 5 to a product, so the 5 gifts are never multiplied.

modeling.title: Snacks for the reading party
modeling.scenario: A fictional class plans a reading party. There will be 6 groups, and each group gets some snacks and one juice. The costs are made up for this exercise.

given.label: Cost of one juice for each group

assumptions: Every group gets the same number of snacks and one juice.
The prices do not change during the week.
There are no coupons and no extra fees.
prompts: Write an expression for the cost for one group. Then write one for all 6 groups.
Evaluate your expression for all 6 groups, and show each step in order.
How would your expression change if each group got 5 snacks?
limits: Real prices can change, so the total on the day may be a little different.
Some students may want a second snack, which this expression does not include.

sentence.because: The expression 5 × (4 + 1) equals 25 because the parentheses say to add 4 + 1 = 5 first, and then multiply 5 × 5.
sentence.but: The expression 5 × 4 + 1 uses the same numbers, but it equals 21.
sentence.so: The parentheses group 4 + 1, so the expression 5 × (4 + 1) equals 25.

diagnostic.prompt: Write an expression for 'add 6 and 3, then multiply by 4'. Evaluate it, then tell what would change if the parentheses were removed.
lookFor: Writes (6 + 3) × 4 with the parentheses in the right place
Evaluates it as 36
Explains that without parentheses 3 × 4 happens first, so the value is 18
diagnostic.language: Let the student act out the steps with counters or a drawing before writing. If the student can show the steps but cannot write the expression, the barrier is language, not the order of operations.

extension.task: Use the numbers 2, 3 and 4 exactly once each, with the signs + and ×, to make one expression equal to 20 and another equal to 14.
extension.reasoning: Explain why 3 × (4 + 2) and 3 × 4 + 2 cannot have the same value, without evaluating either one.

en.learning: Your child is learning to write and solve number expressions with parentheses, like 5 × (4 + 1), and to do the steps in the right order.
en.say: Do what is inside the parentheses first. Then multiply and divide before you add and subtract.
en.ask: What is 3 + 4 × 2? What changes if we write (3 + 4) × 2?
en.activity: Write the cost of a snack for the family as an expression, like 4 × (2 + 1) for 4 people who each buy a fruit cup for 2 dollars and a drink for 1 dollar. Ask your child to say each step.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a escribir y resolver expresiones numéricas con paréntesis, como 5 × (4 + 1), y a hacer los pasos en el orden correcto.
es.say: Primero hagan lo que está dentro de los paréntesis. Después multipliquen y dividan antes de sumar y restar.
es.activity: Escriban el costo de una merienda para la familia como una expresión, por ejemplo 4 × (2 + 1) para 4 personas que compran una fruta de 2 dólares y una bebida de 1 dólar. Pidan a su hijo o hija que diga cada paso.

skills.objective: Students generate two numerical patterns from two given rules, write corresponding terms as ordered pairs, and describe the relationship between the terms of the two patterns.
skills.studentObjective: I can make two patterns from two rules and tell how the matching numbers are related.
skills.languageObjective: I will describe how two patterns are related using because, but and so with the words rule, corresponding terms and ordered pair.
successCriteria: I use a rule to build a pattern, starting from the first number.
I match the terms in the same position of two patterns and call them corresponding terms.
I write corresponding terms as ordered pairs with the first pattern's term first.
I describe how the terms of one pattern compare with the terms of the other, and test it on every pair.
skills.bigIdea: Two patterns built from rules can be linked, because the terms in the same position are related in a way that stays the same all the way along.

syntax: Each term in Pattern B is ___ times the matching term in Pattern A.
The rule for the pattern is to start at ___ and ___ each time.
discourse: Describe a relationship and test it on more than one pair
Say a rule as a set of instructions in order

domains.listening: Students listen to a description of two tile borders and write the ordered pair for one step.
domains.speaking: Students say each rule as an instruction and tell a partner how the matching terms compare.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about two savers and underline the rule for each pattern.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about the relationship between two patterns.

vocab.def: A list of numbers or shapes that follows a rule.
vocab.nonExample: 0, 3, 7, 8, 20, which follows no rule
vocab.sentence: The pattern grows by 3 each step.

vocab.def: A statement that tells the starting number and how to get each next number.
vocab.example: Start at 0 and add 3
vocab.nonExample: A list of numbers with no starting number and no change
vocab.sentence: The rule tells me what to do at each step.
vocab.everyday: A law that tells people what they must or must not do

vocab.def: One number in a pattern, named by its position.
vocab.example: In 0, 3, 6, 9, the third term is 6
vocab.nonExample: The fall term at school, which is a period of time
vocab.sentence: The fourth term in my pattern is 9.
vocab.everyday: A part of the school year, such as the fall term

vocab.def: Terms that are in the same position in two patterns.
vocab.example: 9 and 18, which are both the third week's savings
vocab.nonExample: 9 and 12, which are two terms from the same pattern
vocab.sentence: I list the corresponding terms in a table.

vocab.def: Two numbers in a certain order, written in parentheses, that name one pair of terms or a point.
vocab.example: (9, 18) puts the term from the first pattern first
vocab.nonExample: (18, 9), which switches the order
vocab.sentence: I write each pair of corresponding terms as an ordered pair.

misconceptions.belief: If a relationship works for the first pair of terms, it works for all of them.
misconceptions.why: Students find a quick difference between the first two numbers and do not test it on later pairs.
misconceptions.fix: Make a table of at least four pairs and test the relationship on each one before writing it as a rule.

errorCase.story: Ben has two patterns. Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 3. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 6.
steps: Pattern A is 0, 3, 6, 9. Pattern B is 0, 6, 12, 18.
The first pair of non-zero terms is 3 and 6, and 6 is 3 more than 3.
So every term in Pattern B is 3 more than the matching term in Pattern A.
errorCase.explain: Check the next pair: 6 and 12. Here 12 is 6 more than 6, not 3 more. The terms in Pattern B are 2 times the matching terms in A, because 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12 and 9 × 2 = 18.

misconceptions.belief: After the second term, a rule always goes back to adding the first number.
misconceptions.why: Students see the first step of a multiplying pattern as an addition fact and keep using the first change they noticed.
misconceptions.fix: Say the rule aloud before each term, such as 'times 2' every time, and use a table to record what was done to get each term.

errorCase.story: Zoe builds a pattern with the rule: start at 3 and multiply by 2.
steps: The rule is start at 3 and multiply by 2.
The first term is 3 and the second term is 3 × 2 = 6.
The third term is 6 + 3 = 9, because I keep adding 3.
So the pattern is 3, 6, 9, 12.
errorCase.explain: The rule multiplies each term by 2 to get the next one. The third term is 6 × 2 = 12 and the fourth is 12 × 2 = 24, so the pattern is 3, 6, 12, 24.

misconceptions.belief: Ordered pairs come from neighboring terms in the same pattern.
misconceptions.why: Students are used to looking at how one list grows from one term to the next, so they pair terms that are side by side.
misconceptions.fix: Put the two patterns in a table with one row for each position, and make each ordered pair from one row.

errorCase.story: Mei makes ordered pairs from the add-3 pattern 0, 3, 6, 9 and the add-6 pattern 0, 6, 12, 18.
steps: Corresponding terms are the terms in the same position in the two patterns.
I pair neighbors in the first pattern: (0, 3), (3, 6) and (6, 9).
So those are my ordered pairs.
errorCase.explain: Corresponding terms come from the two patterns, one from each: (0, 0), (3, 6), (6, 12) and (9, 18). Neighbors in one pattern show how that pattern grows, not how the two patterns compare.

misconceptions.belief: A rule is a command about what students must do, not a way to build a pattern.
misconceptions.why: The word rule is heard every day for classroom behavior, so students do not hear it as the instructions that build the terms.
misconceptions.fix: Say the rule as a recipe, 'start at 0, then add 3, again and again', and let students follow it with counters.

reading.title: Saving for the Class Trip
reading.text: Hana and her brother Teo are saving coins for a class trip. Hana starts with 0 dollars and follows the rule add 3 dollars each week. Teo starts with 0 dollars and follows the rule add 6 dollars each week. Each list of savings is a pattern. Hana's terms are 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12. Teo's terms are 0, 6, 12, 18 and 24. The terms from the same week are corresponding terms, such as 9 and 18 in week 3. Hana writes them as an ordered pair, (9, 18). She notices that each of Teo's terms is 2 times her matching term. His rule makes the pattern grow twice as fast as hers.
reading.simple: Hana and Teo save coins. Hana starts with 0 dollars and adds 3 dollars each week. Teo starts with 0 dollars and adds 6 dollars each week. Hana's pattern is 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12. Teo's pattern is 0, 6, 12, 18 and 24. The terms from the same week are corresponding terms, like 9 and 18 in week 3. The ordered pair is (9, 18). Each of Teo's terms is 2 times Hana's term.

questions.q: How many dollars does Teo have in week 3?
questions.a: 18 dollars

questions.q: Why do 9 and 18 make a pair of corresponding terms?
questions.a: They are both from week 3, so they are in the same position in the two patterns.

questions.q: How does each of Teo's terms compare with Hana's matching term?
questions.a: It is 2 times as much: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12 and 9 × 2 = 18.

wdntb.why: The first three add the same amount every time. The fourth adds 3 and then 4, so one rule cannot make it.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two patterns: 0, 3, 6, 9 and 0, 6, 12, 18. What do you notice about the numbers in the same position? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If two patterns start at different numbers and add the same amount each time, matching terms stay the same distance apart.
asn.why: Both patterns grow by the same amount each step, so the gap never changes. The patterns 2, 6, 10 and 5, 9, 13 are always 3 apart.

asn.claim: If two patterns both start at 0, each term in the second pattern is twice the matching term in the first.
asn.why: It is true when the second rule adds twice as much, as with add 3 and add 6. It is not true for add 3 and add 9, where each term is 3 times as much.

wyr.q: Would you rather show corresponding terms in a table or as points on a graph?

compare.a: Kai says Pattern B is double Pattern A, because 6 is 3 × 2, 12 is 6 × 2 and 18 is 9 × 2.
compare.b: Lee says Pattern B is always 3 more than Pattern A, because 6 is 3 more than 3.
compare.prompt: Which relationship works for every pair? How can you test it?

debate.claim: Two patterns that both go up are always related by multiplying.
debate.forEvidence: The patterns 0, 3, 6, 9 and 0, 6, 12, 18 are related by multiplying by 2.
debate.againstEvidence: The patterns 2, 6, 10 and 5, 9, 13 are related by adding 3, not by multiplying.

listening.script: Listen to Priya's plan for two tile borders. Border A starts with zero tiles and adds four tiles at each step. Its terms are zero, four, eight, twelve. Border B starts with zero tiles and adds eight tiles at each step. Its terms are zero, eight, sixteen, twenty-four. Priya lines up the terms from step two, eight and sixteen. She writes the ordered pair eight, sixteen, with the first border first. Then she sees that every term in Border B is two times the matching term in Border A, because eight is two times four.

tasks.q: Which ordered pair does Priya write for step two?
tasks.why: At step two Border A has 8 tiles and Border B has 16, and she writes Border A first.

tasks.q: What relationship does Priya find between the two borders?
options: Each term in Border B is 2 times the matching term in Border A.
Each term in Border B is 4 more than the matching term in Border A.
Each term in Border B is half of the matching term in Border A.
tasks.why: 8 is 2 × 4, 16 is 2 × 8, and 24 is 2 × 12. The gap of 4 does not stay the same.

story.title: The Growing Bracelets
story.goal: make two bracelet designs that grow together row by row
story.intro: Sana is designing two bead bracelets for the art show. Each bracelet grows by a rule, and Sana wants the matching rows of the two bracelets to be linked in a clear way.

beats.lead: Sana writes the rule for the first bracelet and begins to build the pattern of beads.
beats.success: Sana follows the rule from the starting number and builds the first bracelet correctly.
beats.redirect: A row has the wrong number of beads, so Sana says the rule again and checks the row before it.

beats.lead: She builds the second bracelet and lines up the rows next to the first one.
beats.success: Sana matches the rows in the same position and writes the corresponding terms in a table.
beats.redirect: The rows do not match, so Sana checks that she paired terms from the same position.

beats.lead: A visitor asks how the two bracelets are connected.
beats.success: Sana tests her idea on every row and states the relationship in one clear sentence.
beats.redirect: Her idea only fits one row, so Sana tests it on the other pairs and changes it.

story.ending: The two bracelets shine side by side, and Sana can explain exactly how their patterns are linked.

panels.says: My pattern starts at 0 and adds 2: 0, 2, 4, 6.
Mine starts at 0 and adds 10: 0, 10, 20, 30.
Let us list the corresponding terms: 2 and 10, 4 and 20, 6 and 30.
Every term of mine is 5 times the matching term of yours!

predict.q: Before Mia answers, predict the next ordered pair after (6, 30).
predict.why: Mia's pattern adds 2 to reach 8, and Deshawn's adds 10 to reach 40. Also 8 × 5 = 40.

transfer.relationship: Each term of the second pattern is 2 times the matching term of the first
phrasings: Teo saves 2 times as much as Hana in every week
The pairs (3, 6), (6, 12) and (9, 18) all have the second number twice the first
B = 2 × A for every pair of corresponding terms
Adding 6 each week grows twice as fast as adding 3 each week

decoys.text: Teo always has 3 more dollars than Hana
decoys.why: The gap grows each week, 3, 6, 9, so it is not always 3.

decoys.text: Hana's terms are 2 times Teo's terms
decoys.why: This reverses the patterns. Hana's terms are half of Teo's terms.

modeling.title: Two walking clubs
modeling.scenario: A fictional school has two walking clubs. Club A walks the same distance every day, and Club B walks a longer distance every day. The distances are made up for this exercise.
assumptions: Both clubs start at 0 kilometers on day 0.
Each club walks exactly its distance every day.
Nobody skips a day in the first 5 days.
prompts: Make a table of the total kilometers for each club on days 0 to 5.
Write four ordered pairs with Club A's total first, and tell how the two totals are related.
On which day has Club B walked 24 kilometers, and how far has Club A walked on that day?
limits: Real walkers do not go exactly the same distance every day.
Bad weather could stop a club, and then the pattern would break.

sentence.base: The terms of Pattern B are twice the terms of Pattern A.
sentence.because: The terms of Pattern B are twice the terms of Pattern A because 6 is 2 times 3, 12 is 2 times 6, and 18 is 2 times 9.
sentence.but: Both patterns start at 0, but Pattern B grows twice as fast as Pattern A.
sentence.so: Pattern B adds twice as much at each step, so its terms are twice the matching terms in Pattern A.

diagnostic.prompt: Start at 0 and add 4 to make Pattern A. Start at 0 and add 8 to make Pattern B. Write the first four pairs of corresponding terms and tell how the two patterns are related.
lookFor: Builds 0, 4, 8, 12 and 0, 8, 16, 24 from the rules
Writes ordered pairs with the term from Pattern A first
States that each term in Pattern B is 2 times the matching term in Pattern A
diagnostic.language: Let the student build both patterns with counters or a table before explaining. If the table is correct but the sentence is hard to produce, the barrier is language, not patterns.

extension.task: Make two patterns that both start at 0 so that each term in the second pattern is 5 times the matching term in the first. Write the two rules.
extension.reasoning: Explain why you can be sure that the 20th term of an add-6 pattern from 0 is twice the 20th term of an add-3 pattern from 0, without writing all the terms.

en.learning: Your child is learning to make two number patterns from two rules and to see how the matching numbers are related, like add 3 and add 6.
en.say: Write both patterns in two rows, one above the other, and look closely at the numbers that line up.
en.ask: One pattern starts at 0 and adds 2. Another starts at 0 and adds 4. What do you notice about the numbers that line up?
en.activity: Count by 2s and by 4s on a hundred chart, using a different color for each. Ask your child what they notice about the numbers that match step by step.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a hacer dos patrones numéricos con dos reglas y a ver cómo se relacionan los números que se corresponden, como sumar 3 y sumar 6.
es.say: Escriban los dos patrones en dos filas, una encima de la otra, y miren con atención los números que quedan alineados.
es.ask: Un patrón empieza en 0 y suma 2. Otro empieza en 0 y suma 4. ¿Qué notas en los números que quedan alineados?
es.activity: Cuenten de 2 en 2 y de 4 en 4 en una tabla del 100, con un color distinto para cada patrón. Pregunten a su hijo o hija qué nota en los números que se corresponden paso a paso.

skills.objective: Students understand volume as the number of unit cubes that fill a solid, find the volume of rectangular prisms by counting layers and by multiplying, and add the volumes of two prisms that make one solid.
skills.studentObjective: I can find how many unit cubes fill a box and explain my work with layers.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I found a volume using because, but and so with the words layer, base and cubic unit.
successCriteria: I say that volume counts the unit cubes that fill a solid with no gaps.
I find the number of cubes in one layer and multiply by the number of layers.
I write the volume with cubic units, not square units.
I find the volume of a solid made of two prisms by adding the two volumes.
skills.bigIdea: Volume is the number of unit cubes that fill a solid, so it is found by counting how many cubes are in one layer and how many layers there are.

syntax: One layer has ___ cubes and there are ___ layers, so the volume is ___.
The volume is ___ cubic units, not square units, because ___.
discourse: Explain a measurement by describing the layers in order
Compare two different boxes that have the same volume

domains.listening: Students listen to a model-tank description and name the cubes in one layer and the unit for the volume.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how many cubes are in a layer, how many layers there are, and what the unit is.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about packing boxes and mark each measurement with the dimension it names.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that explains a volume.

vocab.def: The amount of space inside a solid shape, measured in cubic units.
vocab.example: A box that holds 24 unit cubes has a volume of 24 cubic units
vocab.nonExample: How loud the music is
vocab.sentence: The volume of the box is 24 cubic units.
vocab.everyday: How loud a sound is, or one book in a set of books
vocab.morphology: from Latin volumen, meaning a roll or a scroll

vocab.def: A cube whose edges are each 1 unit long, used to measure volume.
vocab.example: A cube with edges that are each 1 centimeter long
vocab.nonExample: A cube with edges that are each 2 centimeters long
vocab.sentence: I fill the box with unit cubes.

vocab.def: The unit for volume: the space taken up by one unit cube.
vocab.example: 1 cubic centimeter
vocab.nonExample: 1 square centimeter, which measures flat area
vocab.sentence: I write the volume in cubic units.

vocab.def: One flat level of unit cubes that covers the base of a solid.
vocab.example: A layer of 12 cubes in a box that is 4 cubes long and 3 cubes wide
vocab.nonExample: A single cube standing alone
vocab.sentence: Each layer has the same number of cubes.
vocab.everyday: One thickness of something, such as a layer of cake or a layer of clothing

vocab.def: The face of a solid that the layers sit on; its area tells the cubes in one layer.
vocab.example: A box with a base that is 4 cubes by 3 cubes
vocab.nonExample: The top face of the box
vocab.sentence: The base of the box has 12 square units of area.
vocab.everyday: A safe spot that a runner touches in a game such as baseball

misconceptions.belief: To find volume, add the length, the width and the height.
misconceptions.why: Students know that measurements can be added to find a distance around, and they do not yet picture the cubes that fill the inside.
misconceptions.fix: Build a small box from unit cubes, count one layer, then count the layers, and compare the count with the sum of the edges.

errorCase.story: Pia wants the volume of a box that is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall.
steps: The box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall.
I add the three measurements: 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
So the volume is 12 cubic centimeters.
errorCase.explain: Volume counts the cubes that fill the box. One layer holds 5 × 4 = 20 cubes, and there are 3 layers, so the volume is 20 × 3 = 60 cubic centimeters.

misconceptions.belief: The volume of a box is written in square units.
misconceptions.why: Students have measured area with square units for a long time, so they use the same unit even when the number comes from three measurements.
misconceptions.fix: Hold a flat square tile next to a unit cube and ask which one can be stacked to fill a box.

errorCase.story: Leo finds the volume of a box that is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 2 cm tall.
steps: The box is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 2 cm tall.
I multiply 6 × 2 × 2 = 24.
So the volume is 24 square centimeters.
errorCase.explain: The number 24 is right, but the unit is not. Volume counts cubes, so the volume is 24 cubic centimeters. Square centimeters measure flat area.

misconceptions.belief: When a solid is made of two prisms, multiply their volumes to get the total.
misconceptions.why: Students have just learned that volume comes from multiplying, so they multiply again when they combine two parts.
misconceptions.fix: Build the solid from two sets of cubes and count them together, so the total is clearly how many cubes there are in all.

errorCase.story: Amir finds the volume of an L-shaped solid made of one prism that is 5 by 2 by 3 and one prism that is 2 by 2 by 3.
steps: The solid is made of two prisms: 5 × 2 × 3 and 2 × 2 × 3.
The first volume is 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 and the second is 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
I multiply the two volumes: 30 × 12 = 360 cubic units.
errorCase.explain: The two prisms are parts of one solid, so their cubes are counted together. Add the volumes: 30 + 12 = 42 cubic units.

misconceptions.belief: Volume is how loud something is, so it cannot measure a box.
misconceptions.why: Students hear volume most often about music and screens, so the geometry meaning feels like a different word.
misconceptions.fix: Put two meanings side by side on a poster, with a speaker and a box of cubes, and ask which one fits each sentence.

reading.title: Packing the Boxes
reading.text: Omar is packing a small box with wooden unit cubes. Each unit cube is 1 centimeter long, wide and tall. The base of the box is 5 centimeters by 4 centimeters, so one layer holds 5 × 4 = 20 cubes. The box is 3 layers tall. Omar finds the volume by multiplying 20 × 3 = 60. The volume is 60 cubic units, or 60 cubic centimeters. His sister's box has a base of 6 centimeters by 2 centimeters and is 5 layers tall. Its volume is 6 × 2 × 5 = 60 cubic centimeters. The boxes look different, but they hold the same number of cubes.
reading.simple: Omar packs a box with unit cubes. Each unit cube is 1 centimeter long, wide and tall. The base is 5 centimeters by 4 centimeters. One layer holds 5 × 4 = 20 cubes. The box is 3 layers tall. The volume is 20 × 3 = 60 cubic centimeters. His sister's box has a base of 6 centimeters by 2 centimeters and is 5 layers tall. Its volume is 6 × 2 × 5 = 60 cubic centimeters. The boxes look different, but the volume is the same.

questions.q: How many unit cubes fit in one layer of Omar's box?
questions.a: 20 cubes

questions.q: Why does Omar multiply 20 by 3?
questions.a: There are 3 layers, and each layer has 20 cubes.

questions.q: Do the two boxes have the same volume? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes. 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 and 6 × 2 × 5 = 60, so both have a volume of 60 cubic centimeters.

wdntb.why: 24 square units measures flat area. The other three can all describe the volume of a box that holds 24 cubes.

noticeWonder.prompt: A box is filled with 3 layers of cubes. Each layer has 4 rows with 5 cubes in every row. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If you double the height of a box and keep the same base, the volume doubles.
asn.why: Doubling the height gives twice as many layers, and every layer has the same number of cubes.

asn.claim: A box with a greater length has a greater volume than another box.
asn.why: Length alone does not decide. A 6 by 1 by 1 box holds 6 cubes, but a 3 by 3 by 3 box holds 27 cubes.

wyr.q: Would you rather find a volume by building it with cubes or by multiplying the three measurements?

compare.a: Nia finds the volume of a 4 by 3 by 2 box by finding the base, 4 × 3 = 12, and then multiplying by the height: 12 × 2 = 24.
compare.b: Raj finds the volume of the same box by adding: 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
compare.prompt: Which strategy gives the volume? How do you know?

debate.claim: The volume of any solid is found by multiplying length, width and height.
debate.forEvidence: A box that is 5 by 4 by 3 has a volume of 5 × 4 × 3 = 60, and this works for every rectangular prism.
debate.againstEvidence: An L-shaped solid is not one prism, so you must split it into prisms and add their volumes.

listening.script: Listen to Marisol explain her model fish tank. My tank is a rectangular prism. The base is eight centimeters by three centimeters. I fill one layer with unit cubes, and that layer takes twenty-four cubes. My tank is four layers tall, so I need four groups of twenty-four. Twenty-four times four is ninety-six. The volume of my tank is ninety-six cubic centimeters. It is not ninety-six square centimeters, because square units cover a flat surface, and cubes fill space.

tasks.q: How many unit cubes are in one layer of Marisol's tank?
tasks.why: The base is 8 by 3, so one layer holds 8 × 3 = 24 cubes.

tasks.q: Which unit does Marisol use for the volume?
tasks.why: Cubes fill space, so the volume is in cubic centimeters.

story.title: The Storeroom Move
story.goal: choose the right boxes to move the class books to the new reading room
story.intro: The library is moving to a new reading room. Dalia has boxes of different sizes, and she needs to know how many book-sized cubes each box can hold before the movers arrive.

beats.lead: Dalia opens the first box and looks at the bottom to see how many cubes fit in one layer.
beats.success: Dalia counts the cubes on the base and finds the number in one layer.
beats.redirect: The layer count looks off, so Dalia checks the rows and columns on the base again.

beats.lead: She stacks layers in a second box and wants to know how many cubes fill it.
beats.success: Dalia multiplies the cubes in one layer by the number of layers and writes the volume with cubic units.
beats.redirect: The unit on her label is wrong, so Dalia checks whether she is counting cubes or covering a flat face.

beats.lead: A bookcase shaped like an L has to be packed, so Dalia must find its volume in two parts.
beats.success: Dalia splits the L into two prisms and adds their volumes to get the total.
beats.redirect: The total seems too large, so Dalia checks that she added the parts instead of multiplying them.

story.ending: Every box is packed, the labels are right, and Dalia can explain how each volume was found.

panels.says: My box is 5 by 2 by 4. I add the measurements, so the volume is 5 + 2 + 4 = 11 cubic units.
Volume counts the cubes that fill the box, not the edges. How many cubes are in one layer?
The base is 5 by 2, so one layer has 10 cubes.
There are 4 layers, so 10 × 4 = 40 cubic units.

predict.q: Before Elena answers, predict the volume of Tobi's box.
predict.why: One layer has 5 × 2 = 10 cubes, and 4 layers hold 10 × 4 = 40 cubes.

transfer.relationship: A box with 12 cubes in each layer and 3 layers holds 36 cubes
phrasings: 12 cubes in each layer and 3 layers
4 × 3 × 3 = 36 cubic units
A base area of 12 square units times a height of 3 units
36 unit cubes fill the box with no gaps

decoys.why: This adds the edge lengths, but volume counts how many cubes fill the inside.
This adds the base area and the height instead of multiplying the cubes in a layer by the number of layers.

modeling.title: Soil for a herb planter
modeling.scenario: A fictional class builds a rectangular planter for herbs and has to buy soil. The measurements and the size of the soil bags are made up for this exercise.
assumptions: The inside of the planter is a rectangular prism.
The soil fills the planter to exactly the depth given.
Every bag holds exactly 2 cubic feet of soil.
prompts: How many cubic feet of soil does the planter hold?
How many bags of soil does the class need?
What would change if the soil depth were 2 feet instead of 1 foot?
limits: Soil settles after watering, so the planter may need a little more soil.
Real bags are never filled to exactly the same amount.

sentence.base: The volume of the box is 60 cubic units.
sentence.because: The volume of the box is 60 cubic units because one layer has 5 × 4 = 20 unit cubes and there are 3 layers.
sentence.but: The two boxes have different bases, but both have a volume of 60 cubic units.
sentence.so: One layer holds 20 unit cubes and there are 3 layers, so the volume is 60 cubic units.

diagnostic.prompt: Show how to find the volume of a box that is 4 units long, 3 units wide and 2 units tall. Say the unit you use.
lookFor: Finds 12 cubes in one layer from the base
Multiplies by 2 layers to get 24
Names the unit as cubic units, not square units
diagnostic.language: Let the student build the box with cubes or draw the layers before explaining. If the count is right and the sentence is short, the barrier is language, not volume.

extension.task: An L-shaped solid is made of a prism that is 4 by 2 by 3 and a prism that is 2 by 2 by 3 joined together. Find its volume.
extension.reasoning: Show two different ways to split an L-shaped solid into prisms, and explain why both give the same volume.

en.learning: Your child is learning that volume is the number of cubes that fill a box, found by multiplying the length, the width and the height.
en.say: Think in layers. Count how many cubes fit on the bottom, then count how many layers there are.
en.ask: A box has 6 cubes in one layer and 3 layers. How many cubes fill it?
en.activity: Use a small box and building blocks or dice that are all the same size. Fill one layer, count it, and ask how many cubes fill the whole box.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que el volumen es el número de cubos que llenan una caja, y que se halla multiplicando el largo, el ancho y la altura.
es.say: Piensen en capas. Cuenten cuántos cubos caben en el fondo y después cuántas capas hay.
es.ask: Una caja tiene 6 cubos en una capa y 3 capas. ¿Cuántos cubos la llenan?
es.activity: Usen una caja pequeña y bloques o dados del mismo tamaño. Llenen una capa, cuéntenla y pregunten cuántos cubos llenan toda la caja.

skills.objective: Students graph and name points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane using ordered pairs, and solve problems by plotting points and finding distances along grid lines.
skills.studentObjective: I can plot a point from an ordered pair, name a point on a graph, and find how far apart two points are.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain where a point is using because, but and so with the words ordered pair, origin and coordinate.
successCriteria: I start at the origin and move right first, then up, to plot an ordered pair.
I name a plotted point with an ordered pair in the correct order.
I tell the difference between the x-axis and the y-axis.
I find the distance between two points on the same vertical or horizontal line.
skills.bigIdea: An ordered pair is a set of directions from the origin, so the order of the two numbers decides which point it names.

syntax: To plot ___, I move ___ units right and ___ units up from the origin.
The points ___ and ___ are different because the order of the coordinates matters.
discourse: Give directions to a point in the right order
Explain why two ordered pairs with the same numbers name different points

domains.listening: Students listen to directions for plotting a point and show with a finger where the point is on a grid.
domains.speaking: Students give a partner directions such as right 4, up 2, and name the point with an ordered pair.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage about a map on a coordinate plane and circle each ordered pair with the place it names.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about two points with the same numbers in different orders.

vocab.def: A flat surface that goes on forever in every direction.
vocab.example: The coordinate plane is a flat grid of points
vocab.nonExample: A ball, which is round and not flat
vocab.sentence: I plot each point on the coordinate plane.
vocab.everyday: An aircraft with wings, or a tool for smoothing wood

vocab.def: The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and the y-axis meet.
vocab.example: The front gate at (0, 0)
vocab.nonExample: The point (4, 2)
vocab.sentence: I start every move at the origin.
vocab.morphology: from Latin origo, meaning a beginning

vocab.def: A number line used to locate points; the plane has an x-axis and a y-axis.
vocab.example: The x-axis runs left to right
vocab.nonExample: A line drawn at a slant across the plane
vocab.sentence: The x-axis is the horizontal axis.
vocab.morphology: the plural is axes, said AK-seez

vocab.def: Two numbers in a set order, such as (4, 2), that name one point on the plane.
vocab.example: (4, 2) is 4 units right and 2 units up
vocab.nonExample: The numbers 4 and 2 listed in any order
vocab.sentence: Each point has its own ordered pair.

vocab.def: One number in an ordered pair; it tells how far to move along an axis.
vocab.example: In (4, 2), the x-coordinate is 4
vocab.nonExample: The whole pair (4, 2), which has two coordinates
vocab.sentence: The second coordinate tells how far up to move.

misconceptions.belief: The first number in an ordered pair tells how far to go up.
misconceptions.why: Students read a graph from the top, or they use the order of the numbers without knowing which axis each one belongs to.
misconceptions.fix: Label the axes, and say a short rule such as 'run along the hallway first, then climb the stairs' each time a point is plotted.

errorCase.story: Cam plots the ordered pair (4, 2) on a coordinate plane.
steps: The ordered pair is (4, 2).
I start at the origin, move up 4 units, and then move right 2 units.
So I plot the point at (2, 4).
errorCase.explain: The first coordinate tells how far to move right along the x-axis, so move right 4 and then up 2. That point is at (4, 2).

misconceptions.belief: To find the distance between two points, count the numbers from one point to the other, including both.
misconceptions.why: Students count objects by touching each one, so they count the endpoints too instead of the jumps between them.
misconceptions.fix: Draw the jumps on a number line and show that the distance is the number of equal steps, not the number of marks.

errorCase.story: Sofia finds how far apart the points (2, 3) and (2, 8) are.
steps: The points (2, 3) and (2, 8) are on the same vertical line.
I count the numbers from 3 to 8: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, which is 6 numbers.
So the distance is 6 units.
errorCase.explain: Distance counts the jumps between the points, not the points. The jumps are 8 − 3 = 5, so the distance is 5 units.

misconceptions.belief: Any point with a 0 in its ordered pair sits on the x-axis.
misconceptions.why: Students link the number zero with the starting line they know best, the horizontal one, and do not check which coordinate is zero.
misconceptions.fix: Plot (5, 0) and (0, 5) side by side and ask which direction each point moved from the origin.

errorCase.story: Jin looks at the point (0, 5) on a coordinate plane.
steps: The first coordinate of (0, 5) is 0, so the point moves 0 units right.
The second coordinate is 5, so the point moves 5 units up.
Since the point has a 0 in it, it is on the x-axis.
errorCase.explain: The point is 5 units straight up from the origin, so it is on the y-axis. A point on the x-axis has a second coordinate of 0, like (5, 0).

misconceptions.belief: The word axes is about axes for chopping wood, so there is only one axis on a graph.
misconceptions.why: The plural of axis is spelled and said differently from the plural of ax, so the word is easy to mishear.
misconceptions.fix: Say axis and axes aloud with a drawing of two crossing number lines, and point to each line as you say the word.

reading.title: Mapping the School Yard
reading.text: The garden club draws a map of the school yard on a coordinate plane. The origin, (0, 0), is the front gate. Each ordered pair names one place. The first coordinate tells how far to move right along the x-axis. The second coordinate tells how far to move up along the y-axis. The bike rack is at (4, 2), so it is 4 units right and 2 units up from the gate. The water tap is at (2, 4). It has the same numbers in a different order, so it is a different place. The sandbox is at (4, 7), straight above the bike rack. The distance between them is 7 − 2 = 5 units.
reading.simple: The garden club draws a map on a coordinate plane. The origin, (0, 0), is the gate. The first coordinate tells how far to move right on the x-axis. The second coordinate tells how far to move up on the y-axis. The bike rack is at (4, 2). The water tap is at (2, 4). The numbers are the same, but the order is different, so the places are different. The sandbox is at (4, 7), straight above the bike rack. The distance is 7 − 2 = 5 units.

questions.q: Where is the bike rack on the map?
questions.a: At (4, 2), which is 4 units right and 2 units up from the gate

questions.q: Why are (4, 2) and (2, 4) different places on the map?
questions.a: The first coordinate is how far right and the second is how far up, so changing the order moves the point.

questions.q: How far is the sandbox from the bike rack, and how do you know?
